title: Beyond Prompts: Measuring and Optimizing LLM Tool-Agent Harnesses
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 4 Sep 2026 (v1), last revised 9 Sep 2026 (this version, v2)]
    Title:Beyond Prompts: Measuring and Optimizing LLM Tool-Agent Harnesses
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:LLM tool agents can be improved without retraining by modifying the runtime harness around a fixed model: prompts, tool interfaces, middleware, state handling, and recovery logic. We study this setting as resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model multi-turn tool agents, with the search surface scoped to prompts and tool-boundary middleware: edits are guarded intercepts at the tool boundary, not arbitrary rewriting of agent execution logic. Our optimizer-agnostic protocol reports mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, logged cost diagnostics, and RelLift95(B), a conservative estimate of the held-out gain of the harness selected under budget B. We instantiate the protocol with prompt-only and prompt-plus-middleware optimizers, including PRISM, which clusters failures and routes repairs to prompt, tool-boundary middleware, or joint edit surfaces within a Pareto search. On BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom, PRISM obtains mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points and positive empirical RelLift95 on all three benchmarks, and a component ablation attributes the margin chiefly to failure-surface routing and the edit-pattern constraint. Across optimizers, the results show that some search procedures can occasionally find large gains but still choose brittle updates, so the reliability of the chosen harness should be reported alongside average held-out lift.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper proposes a protocol and optimizer (PRISM) for measuring and improving LLM tool-agent harnesses — prompts, tool interfaces, and middleware — yielding up to ~15-point benchmark gains without retraining.
report.background: Tool-using LLM agents now power coding assistants, customer-service bots, and workflow automation. Teams typically improve them by upgrading the base model, which is costly, or by hand-tuning prompts, which is brittle. But agent success in multi-turn tasks depends heavily on the runtime 'harness': tool schemas, tool-boundary middleware, state handling, and recovery logic. Harness tuning has historically been ad hoc and unreproducible, with reported gains rarely accompanied by uncertainty estimates, so improvements often fail to survive production. Standardized multi-turn benchmarks such as BFCL and tau2 (Retail/Telecom) now let researchers compare harness edits systematically. This paper formalizes harness selection as a resource-bounded search problem under a fixed model, and argues that reliability of the chosen harness must be reported alongside average lift.
key_points: The paper targets a fixed model and only edits its runtime harness — prompts, tool interfaces, middleware, state handling, and recovery logic. No retraining or weight updates are required, making the approach cheap and immediately applicable to deployed agents.

The search surface is deliberately restricted: edits are guarded intercepts at the tool boundary rather than arbitrary rewrites of agent execution logic. This constraint keeps changes safe, composable, and easier to reason about in production systems.

The authors propose an optimizer-agnostic evaluation protocol reporting mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, logged cost diagnostics, and RelLift95(B), a conservative estimate of held-out gain for the harness selected under budget B.

PRISM clusters failures and routes repairs to prompt edits, tool-boundary middleware, or joint edits within a Pareto search. It achieves mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points on BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom, with positive RelLift95 on all three.

An ablation attributes PRISM's margin mainly to failure-surface routing and the edit-pattern constraint. Across optimizers, some search procedures occasionally find large gains but still select brittle updates — so reported averages alone can be misleading.

The core methodological message is that harness selection should be treated as a reliability-aware optimization problem, not a one-shot prompt-tuning exercise, with budget, variance, and worst-case behavior made explicit.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this shifts agent improvement away from expensive model retraining toward reproducible harness optimization — a cheaper, faster lever that could become standard practice for shipping agents. Developers gain a template for evaluating harness changes: report worst-case lift, repeatability, and conservative lower bounds, not just best-run numbers, which should reduce fragile prompt hacks reaching production. It also suggests tool-interface middleware is a first-class design surface. For regular users, the benefit is more dependable multi-turn agents that fail less often on tasks like retail ordering or telecom support. The main caveat is that results are benchmark-based; real-world distribution shift and cost budgets may tell a different story.
report.tools: BFCL (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard) and tau2-bench (Retail/Telecom) are the evaluation suites used here and are open for reproducing harness tests. For building and editing harnesses, watch DSPy for programmatic prompt optimization, LangGraph and the OpenAI Agents SDK for middleware, state, and recovery hooks, and MCP (Model Context Protocol) for standardized tool interfaces. If the authors release PRISM code, it would be the most direct artifact to try; otherwise track the arXiv ID on alphaXiv and Hugging Face Papers for code links and discussion.
